utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Can we have the case called on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-98-32/1-R77.2, The Prosecutor versus Jelena Rasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Kyle Wood and Aditya Menon for the Prosecution, along with our Case Manager, Jasmina Bosnjakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Defence counsel, Mira Tapuskovic, Defence counsel for Jelena Rasic, and my assistant --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. And we all know that the accused is not present and excused from being present. While I'm dealing with that, I'd simply like to orally deal with the Defence motion for modifications on the conditions under which she is under provision release. Pursuant to the decision of the 12th of November, 2010, she was to reside in the home of her parents in Belgrade, remain within the confines of the city of Belgrade and report to the local police station. The Defence sought through their motion to have those three conditions modified to allow for the accused to travel, along with her parents, to their country home in Cerovac village, in the municipal of Smederevska Palanka, to reside and remain within that jurisdiction for the duration of her parents' visits, and to report to the designated local police station every Monday and Friday. And the accused additionally undertook to inform local police stations, both in Belgrade and in the municipality in advance of travel. The Prosecution does not object to the request and agrees that the supplementary measure will provide an additional safe-guard. In consequence, the Trial Chamber grants the motion as requested and, in addition, orders the accused to report to the designated local police station in the municipality of Smederevska Palanka upon arrival. And a written decision will follow. Do all parties have the proposed agenda for today's conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Let's go through it. First of all, the pending motion which was to amend the indictment, it struck me that the Prosecution now having filed a pre-trial brief which extensively amplifies the indictment, is there anything now of worth remaining in the preliminary motion to amend the indictment, or can that be subsumed into the pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence's view is that it should be acted upon the guide-lines and instructions issued by you at the Status Conference held on 4th of February this year, and in them, you indicated in what way the indictment should be amended by specifying exactly which wording should be used and which paragraphs and which counts of the indictment should be subject to amendment. The Defence believes that it could be properly discussed about the knowledge of the accused in terms of her providing false testimony [as interpreted], only if the -- she is questioned in accordance with the guide-lines issued by you on the 4th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution stands by what it has said in its response to that motion and agree with Your Honour. At the last Status Conference you said that you believed the indictment does plead a prima facie case, and the Prosecution mentioned at the last Status Conference that we would be filing a pre-trial brief that would, in fact, as you say, amplify these points. I think the Prosecution has done that. The accused is certainly on notice of the case to which she has to answer. And, in particular, paragraphs 56, 61, 66, 71, and 76 of the pre-trial brief, I think, sufficiently answer the concerns of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well the amendments that I suggested at the last Status Conference are very small, and I can't, for myself, see any great difficulty incorporating them into the indictment. I don't want to generate unnecessary work. In reality, is there any part of the Prosecution's case now that the Defence do not understand, i.e., that any part of the allegations that -- in the Defence case that means that the defendant doesn't know which the -- the accused doesn't know what the case is that she has to meet?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I answer your question, I would like to make a small correction. On page 3, in the transcript, line 2, it says her providing false testimony. It should read her providing false statements. Now, Your Honour, if I may respond to your question. The Defence fully understand the indictment, and we see in which direction it is going and in what way it is determining the mens rea of the defendant. We believe that the suggestion that you have made was not a big job for the Prosecution to do in terms of adjusting the indictment since the last Status Conference of the 4th of February. If the Trial Chamber believes that they can be satisfied with the amendment such amended, that is to say, the knowledge about the acts that she undertook and her knowledge about the witness statement being false, then the Defence will not cause any problems in that respect either, and I repeat, provided you are satisfied that this meets the standards and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal in terms of the mens rea of the accused and the comparison with the deeds that they are accused of having committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it is self-evident that I do, because I confirm that the indictment set out a prima facie case. The prima facie case is not an exhaustive definition of the liability or the allegations. But if you couple that indictment together with the Prosecution pre-trial brief, it's abundantly plain what the case is that the accused has to meet. It is abundantly plain what is being said against her, and the elements of mens rea which the Prosecution need to prove, along with the actus reus, so I think we can safely leave the indictment as it is. And the easiest thing, therefore, probably is if the Defence withdraw their preliminary motion, being satisfied that the Trial Chamber is satisfied that all necessary matters are now in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is going to act accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on to pre-trial preparation. Rule 66(A)(ii), what is the position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure is complete, Your Honour, but for two witnesses that are subject to a pending motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... so that motion needs to be addressed. Any observations as to that, Ms. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I can only confirm what the representative of the Prosecution has already said, i.e., that everything cited so far will be used during trial, pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii), disclosed to the Defence in the language understood by the defendant. However, we are maintaining constant contact with the Prosecution, and this is going to be, as we understand, disclosed to the Defence in the shortest possible term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution to file its motion for admission of 92 bis and 92 ter according to the pre-trial witness list. That's in hand, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution is prepared to file those motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Can that be done, please, by -- bearing in mind that there is no way that we are going to be able to have this case listed for trial before the recess, can that be done by the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And also motion to file -- or notice for protective measures for any, if any, by the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution is in the process of investigating that right now. I should mention going back to the 92 bis motion, of course, there are witnesses, the two witnesses I mentioned earlier subject to that as well. So barring that, we can meet the 1 July deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. There has been no objection from the Defence, as I see it, as to the Prosecution expert report under Rule 94 bis. Is that going to remain the same position?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The situation is such that the Defence has not filed a notice to the Trial Chamber, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, due to the fact that we had agreed with the Prosecution on the 2nd of May of this year for the expert report to be included into agreed facts. And we have taken that as an irrefutable piece of evidence, and it is, I think -- that is an irrefutable piece of evidence, number 5, and the Defence believe that the Trial Chamber has been notified about that, and that they will take this as a notice from the Defence, indicating that they have no need to question the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Presumably no difficulty as to that. Any -- any suggestions or modifications? I think we thought, if I recall rightly, that the trial was likely to take three working weeks. Have subsequent events altered either party's estimate for that length?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, it's has been a productive few months, I think, since the last Status Conference, Your Honour. As you know, we have filed a set of agreed exhibits. We have filed a set of agreed facts, 52. Given that, the Prosecution has been able to whittle down its witness list significantly, well, to a certain extent. I think we reported before perhaps 19 witnesses total. We now anticipate perhaps 12 total, and that includes among that the expert witness we just talked about. So presumably that wouldn't be required as well. As you know, we've put forward an estimate of 16 hours for our case in-chief. This obviously also depends on the outcome of the 92 bis and 92 ter motions. That is the status of the Prosecution's case at their prediction at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Which -- as we don't know at the moment whether we're going -- how we're going to be able to accommodate the trial in terms of days of sitting in a week, we probably can't take the actual length of trial much further forward at the moment. Any observations as to that from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, immediately before the beginning of this Status Conference, I had a conversation with my learned friend from the Prosecution, in the hope of defining the schedule for this trial. In the last two months, we communicated almost on a daily basis by exchanging e-mailings, and we established a sort of co-operation regarding irrefutable facts and evidence. And the Prosecution list of witnesses has been considerably reduce, particularly of those who are going to appear here and testify viva voce. However, I still cannot say what the scope of the Defence case is going to be, because that depends on the Prosecution case. But I do believe that the trial will be shorter all together. It may not require three weeks, but I don't think that it can be shorter than two weeks. Now, as I stand here, this is the best estimate I can give you at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that. And I'm grateful for the very mature collegiate co-operation between the parties. We have a number of limiting factors as to being able to take any fixing of the trial date forward at this moment. It's limited in a number of ways. First of all, as the parties well know, the Haradinaj trial is going to be fixed and the sitting -- sitting schedule for that is going to be fixed. And that trial involves a certain conflict between Judges of this Trial Chamber and the Judges of that trial. So the different sitting options that one might not normally think about at the moment are rather difficult to put into any concrete form. I think the best thing I can do is to say that that will be done by e-mail between the parties as soon as practicable, between the Trial Chamber and the parties, when we know better where we sit in terms of judicial availability and court availability. It may be that we will have to be flexible in our sitting options three days a week, weeks on/weeks off, and things of that nature. And that makes it more, I know, difficult for both parties in terms of witness availability and counsels' availability. Are there any absolute bars to availability on the part of witnesses or parties that can be disclosed at this stage; for instance, for the month of September? Can I be told that, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour. The only scheduling concerns for the Prosecution are that Mr. Rogers, who is not here today and asked for me to apologise for that. He is in Courtroom I right now in the Haradinaj case. He is also on this case, as is my colleague, Mr. Menon. Considering the two other Judges are also on that case, that is the -- that is the main consideration for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence, even before having received the agenda for this Status Conference, has undertaken all the steps in compliance with e-mails sent by Ms. Featherstone to both the Defence and the Prosecution to explore and investigate the possibilities of the best possible times that are suitable to witnesses for them to appear. The Defence witnesses said that they prefer that that be at the beginning of September, and that is what the Defence is counting on; that they can begin their case at that time. However, we are going to try and co-ordinate our schedule with all the commitments and scheduling of other parties involved, but the Defence is ready to start by the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is obviously a matter of great importance for everybody, not least the accused, that the trial is conducted as expeditiously as possible. Fortunately, she is not in custody, so the expedition is perhaps not quite as critical as it might otherwise have been. But, nevertheless, we'll move ahead to fix a trial date and schedule as soon as practicable. Are there any other matters that we can usefully deal with now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution did wish to make a motion to admit into evidence the agreed facts and agreed exhibits; that's 16 exhibits. We thought we would make that motion orally and the Defence could be heard from today. I don't anticipate that there be an objection to that. But I thought that's one thing we can do to move things along today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I already said, Your Honour, we discussed this matter immediately before this Status Conference, and this is something that was also the subject of the e-mails that I exchanged with the Prosecution. I absolutely agree that if it is possible for us to finalise this matter and to see how these facts and the evidence in question is going to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, bearing in mind this is a matter which is dealt with by agreement between the parties, I can't, for the life of me, imagine that there would be any judicial disagreement with that. So I'm going to take the radical step of granting the motion for admission and to accelerate the process as far as possible. My judicial colleagues will be informed. No doubt, if there is outrage, I will be the first to know about it. Anything else that can usefully be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution side, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to notify the Chamber and Your Honour about one thing. On the 26th of January, the Defence filed a motion in the Lukic and Lukic case, to the Appellate Chamber, for disclosure of confidential and ex parte material. The Defence did not request full access to ex parte and confidential material from the Lukic and Lukic case but only to that portion that concerns the acts that the judgement is mentioning in a number of paragraphs and number of footnotes. Unfortunately, the Defence has not received any answer whatsoever, since the 26th of January. I believe that this disclosure will not produce any drastic consequences which would force the Defence to make some major steps during the trial. I believe that we are going to receive this from the Appellate Chamber before the summer recess. And before the trial starts, we hope that the Registry, in co-operation with the Prosecution in the Lukic and Lukic case, will single out and select the specific parts of the material to be disclosed to the Defence in order to enable us to prepare ourselves for the beginning of the trial in good time. We have this problem which is troubling the Defence, to a certain extent, but we do hope that this is going to be overcome because we have more than enough time, which is to say, more than two and a half months before the commencement of the trial. Therefore, I believe that that problem can be solved within that period. I only wanted to bring to your attention that this is a problem that the Defence expects to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I appreciate that there is a delay in that matter. I hope it will be resolved, if -- if as we've -- get close to the recess, there is still no resolution, perhaps Ms. Tapuskovic, you could remind the Chamber, and it may be that gentle pressure might be applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Anything else from the administrative point of view? No. So be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Hopefully, we will not need another Status Conference, but if we do, it will have to be before the -- on or before the 7th of October of 2011 when the 120-day period expires. I think we'll just leave it at that for the moment, and be confident that we won't need another Status Conference date. Thank you very much.
